list.listitem: No routine screening is recommended for neuroblastoma. A
Suspect neuroblastoma in children with abdominal mass or bone pain. C
Urine catecholamine metabolites, vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) and homovanillic acid (HVA), are useful for evaluating children with suspected neuroblastoma. B
Treatment depends on the age of the patient, stage of the tumor, and histology of the tumor. A

background.definition: Neuroblastoma is the most common malignant extracranial solid tumor in infancy. It arises from neuroblasts, which invade the adrenal medulla and the sympathetic ganglia of the abdomen. Signs and symptoms vary depending on location of the tumor, and may include abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia, and bone pain.

list.listitem: 6.7 new cases per 100,000 infants per year
1.1 new cases per 100,000 children aged 1 to 15 years old per year
Less than 1 year of age: 35 per million; 10 to 14 years of age: 1 per million
The cause is unknown, although rare familial cases may arise from a hereditary-predisposition locus at chromosome 16p12-13.

A defect in neuroblast maturation during fetal development leads to the malignant transformation of neuroblasts, which migrate throughout the sympathetic nervous system, explaining the multiple organ sites where these tumors occur.
These undifferentiated neuroblasts (Homer-Wright pseudorosettes) implant primarily in the abdominal cavity, although they can involve the pelvis, thorax, neck, and brain.
The tumor is associated with the n-myc oncogene and tumor cell ploidy; if the n-myc oncogene is positive and cells are diploid, then the prognosis is worse.
Routine screening with urinary VMA and HVA does not impact mortality or morbidity and may lead to false positives and unneeded follow-up testing and procedures. A
Suspect neuroblastoma in children with abdominal mass or bone pain. C
Urine catecholamine metabolites, VMA and HVA, are useful for evaluating children with suspected neuroblastoma. C
Tissue biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis and can be made from bone marrow aspirate or a tumor biopsy. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Malignant renal tumor presents as abdominal mass
Malignant liver tumor, usually in patients <3 years of age. Distinguished by abdominal ultrasound
Uncommon in infants. Becomes more common as age increases. Can present with abdominal mass
May present with bone pain and fever. Often have diffuse lymphadenopathy and organomegally
Can occur in any smooth or skeletal muscle. Often presents with abdominal mass
Incidence peaks at 1 year of age and then rises again after 10 years of age. Presents as mass

Diagnosis.Diagnostic_criteria: Diagnosis is based upon having both of the following: (1) Tumor biopsy or bone marrow aspirate/biopsy contains unequivocal tumor cells. (2) Increased serum catecholamines and urinary catecholamine metabolites, such as VMA or HVA.

list.listitem: Common symptoms of neuroblastoma include bone pain and limp, fever, malaise, weight loss, abdominal pain or mass, and back pain. Constipation, urinary retention, difficulty standing or ambulating, stridor, cough, and dysphagia are less common.
Median age at diagnosis is 22 months, with a peak incidence between 2 and 3 years. It is more common in boys.
Rarely, patients may have opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome (jerking movements of the eyes and extremities) or watery diarrhea.

Work-up for a suspected abdominal mass should generally begin with an ultrasound to avoid excessive radiation exposure and progress to CT or MRI if indicated. Guidelines for imaging based staging are shown in .

Urinary catecholamine metabolites such as VMA and HVA are detected in high levels in the majority of patients with neuroblastoma. The ratio of VMA or HVA to serum creatinine are highly sensitive and specific indicators of neuroblastoma.
Optimal cutoffs for interpretation vary by age.
Patients with bony symptoms should begin with plain films and progress to a bone scan or 131 metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scintigraphy.

(18)F-fluoropropylbenzylguanidine (FPBG) positron emisson tomography (PET) imaging may be better than MIBG for detecting bony lesions. Metastases to marrow or liver may cause anemia, thrombocytopenia or leukopenia as well as elevated transaminases and bilirubin.
When liver involvement is extensive, it may impair synthetic function causing prolonged protimes and partial prothrombin times, and decreased serum albumin.
Biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis (see also Diagnostic Criteria).

A risk score was developed and validated to determine the prognosis for patients >18 months at diagnosis with recurrence of Stage 4 neuroblastoma. The risk score was calculated as 0.8221 (if >1 recurrence site) + 0.707 (if recurrence time <18 mos) + 0.570 (if liver metastasis at diagnosis) + 0.438 (if primary tumor recurrence) + 0.253 (if age <42 months). The low risk group was score <= 0.5, moderate risk was >0.5 to <= 1.2, and high risk was score >1.20.
Suspect neuroblastoma in children (especially under age 1) with an abdominal mass.
Initial evaluation should consist of imaging the mass with ultrasound or CT scan. If neuroblastoma is suspected, order VMA or HVA. Bone scan or MIBG study is useful for defining metastasis.
Definitive diagnosis is made after a pathologist review of bony specimen obtained via biopsy.
Staging is essential and is based upon the International Neuroblastoma Staging System ().
Stage I: Surgical resection only. A
Stage II: Surgical resection in children aged 1 year and under. Over the age of 1 year, surgery plus chemotherapy with or without added radiation. A
Stages III and IV: Surgical debulking, then chemotherapy and radiation. Bone marrow transplant in high-risk patients (older children and those with n-myc amplification). A
Stage I does not require drug therapy. However, if patients develop recurrent disease, chemotherapy can be used and the overall survival remains higher than 95%.

The most effective drug agents for patients aged 1 year or older with stage II and greater favorable histology tumors include 4 to 8 cycles of cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, carboplatin, and etoposide.
There is a recognised need to improve outcomes from systemic therapy and an international project is ongoing with a strategy for accelerating new drug development.

The risk of relapse from minimal residual disease after consolidation may be decreased with cis -retinoic acid treatment. However, a Cochrane review only identified a single RCT with 98 patients who had received chemotherapy and were randomized to retinoic acid or no further treatment, and found no difference in outcomes.

There may be an emerging role for immunotherapy, especially for relapsed or refractory high risk neuroblastoma. A study of 27 children with relapsed or refractory neuroblastoma evaluated immunotherapy using chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-expressing T cells targetting disialoganglioside GD2 which is found on tumor cells. Nine children had a complete response and 8 a partial response. Overall 3 year survival was 60%.
Surgical resection of neuroblastoma tumors have demonstrated improved survival. Outcomes in these patients are dependent on tumor stage and histology.
Stage I tumors normally require resection only resulting in good long-term survival.
Stages II, III, and IV tumors may warrant surgery alongside adjuvant chemotherapy and/or radiation.
Surgical intervention in high-risk patients (stage IV and older than 1 year) remains controversial and does not significantly improve disease-free survival.
Image Defined Risk Factors (IDRFs) are associated with higher risk of incomplete surgical resection and higher risk of surgical complications.
For olfactory neuroblastoma, surgical resection plus radiation therapy are the usual recommended therapy. For selected low risk patients surgery alone may be appropriate.

A review of retrospective cohorts with 162 patients treated using minimally invasive surgery (MIS) and 409 using open surgery found a lower rate of recurrence with MIS. However, selection bias is likely, with lower risk patients preferentially selected for MIS. The American Pediatric Surgical Association Cancer Committee endorses MIS for "carefully selected smaller (4-6 cm) image defined risk factor-negative abdominal tumors."

A Cochrane review found 3 RCTs with over 700 patients evaluating the efficacy of high-dose chemotherapy and autologous hematopoietic stem cell rescue for high-risk children with neuroblastoma. Both event-free and overall survival were improved when compared with conventional therapy (HR 0.78, 95% CI 0.67-0.90).

In the highest risk patients, less than 30 years of age, high dose chemotherapy and tandem autologous hematopoetic stem cell transplantation resulted in improved three year event-free survival compared with single transplantation (61.6% vs 48.4%, P = .006, NNT = 7).
Complications include metastases to lymph nodes, bone marrow, eyes, skin, liver, and spinal cord.
The most serious complication of neuroblastoma is cord compression from a paraspinal tumor requiring urgent neurosurgical evaluation ().

Three-year survival is 90% for stage I or IIA/B with favorable histology; 70% to 90% for stage III, non-amplified myc; and 30% for stage III with myc amplification or stage IV/IVS with myc amplification. A
One study of 8 cases of untreated stages I and II tumors reported natural regression of disease in 5 individuals.
The two most important prognostic factors are the stage of the tumor at the time of diagnosis and the age of the patient.
IDRFs can help predict 5 year event-free survival and overall survival. IDRF positive patients have poorer prognosis.
Children in low-risk groups (stage I or IIA/B with favorable histology) have a 90% survival rate 3 years after diagnosis.
Children in intermediate-risk groups (stage III, non-amplified myc) have a 70% to 90% survival rate 3 years after diagnosis.
Children in high-risk groups (stage III with myc amplification, and stage IV/IVS with myc amplification) have a 30% survival rate 3 years after diagnosis.
The outcome is poor for children with advanced-stage disease, even with the use of surgical measures, chemotherapy, and radiation.
Patients are considered "cured" when they remain disease free for 5 years.
MYCN gene amplification is found in about 20% of cases, and is a poor prognostic indicator. It is detectable in cell-free DNA in serum or in tissue.
Myelosuppression, pancytopenia, and decreased renal function are common complications after chemotherapy, thus regular monitoring with a CBC, platelet count, and serum electrolytes is recommended.
As most recurrences occur within 2 years of completing treatment, patients should undergo close surveillance for signs or symptoms of recurrent disease.

feature.caption: Neuroblastoma Staging.
feature.feature_body:
Stage Criteria
Stage I Localized tumor with complete gross resection of tumor and negative ipsilateral lymph nodes
Stage IIA Localized tumor with incomplete gross resection of tumor and negative ipsilateral lymph nodes
Stage IIB Localized tumor with complete or incomplete gross resection of tumor and positive ipsilateral lymph nodes
Stage III Unresectable unilateral tumor infiltrating across the midline with contralateral lymph node involvement
Stage IV Any primary tumor with dissemination to local lymph nodes, bone, bone marrow, liver, skin, and/or other organs
Stage IVS Localized primary tumor in infants age less than 1 year with dissemination to skin, liver, or bone marrow
Adapted from Brodeur GM, Pritchard J, Berthold F, et al. Revisions of the international criteria for neuroblastoma diagnosis, staging, and response to treatment. J Clin Oncol 1993;11:1466-1477.
